results.title: Finite Alperin groups have derived length at most six

results.title: Growth rate of a $k$-element generating family (Kourovka 14.7)

results.summary: Let $\Gamma$ be a group and $S = (s_1, \dots, s_k)$ a family of $k$ elements generating $\Gamma$. results.title: The commutator of an element with an automorphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an automorphism $\varphi$ of a group $G$ and $x \in G$, $\delta_\varphi(x) = x^{-1} \varphi(x)$. Then the predicate $a \mapsto \exists b \in c(a),\ R(a, b)$ is recursively enumerable.

results.title: Multi-stack decidable predicates are exactly the computable predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is computable, that is, $p$ is decidable and its Boolean characteristic function $\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is computable.

results.title: Multi-stack recognizable predicates are exactly the r.e. predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.

results.title: Multi-stack co-recognizable predicates are exactly the co-r.e. predicates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine if and only if its complement $\neg p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $\neg p$ holds is partial recursive.

results.title: Decidable predicates are recognizable by multi-stack machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Decidability by multi-stack machines is closed under complement
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then so is its complement $\neg p$.

results.title: Decidable predicates are co-recognizable by multi-stack machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine, that is, its complement $\neg p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Post's theorem for multi-stack machines
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is both recognizable and co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

results.title: Decidable predicates are closed under conjunction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are both decidable by multi-stack machines, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \wedge q(a)$.

results.title: Decidable predicates are closed under disjunction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are predicates on $\alpha$ that are decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$.

results.title: Recognizable predicates are closed under conjunction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are both recognizable by multi-stack machines, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \wedge q(a)$.

results.title: Recognizable predicates are closed under disjunction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are predicates on $\alpha$ that are recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$.

results.title: Language of a Boolean test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Boolean-valued function $f$ on words over an alphabet $\sigma$, the language of $f$ is the set of words $u$ over $\sigma$ with $f(u) = \mathrm{true}$.

results.title: Membership in a concatenation of languages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ over an alphabet $\sigma$ and a word $w$ over $\sigma$, $w$ lies in the concatenation $L_1 L_2$ if and only if there are words $u$ and $v$ with $w = uv$, $u \in L_1$ and $v \in L_2$.

results.title: Bounded split test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given Boolean tests $f$ and $g$ on words over $\sigma$, a word $w$ and a natural number $n$, the split test is the Boolean value that is true exactly when there is some $i < n$ such that $f$ is true on the prefix of $w$ of length $\min(i, |w|)$ and $g$ is true on the remaining suffix of $w$.

results.title: Decidable languages have computable membership tests
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then there is a computable function $f$ from words over $\sigma$ to Booleans such that $L$ is the language of $f$, that is, the set of words $u$ with $f(u) = \mathrm{true}$.

results.title: Decidable languages are closed under concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are languages over $\sigma$ whose membership predicates are decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then the membership predicate of their concatenation $L_1 L_2 = \{uv : u \in L_1, v \in L_2\}$ is also decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.

results.title: Splits of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $w$ over $\sigma$ of length $n$, this is the list of the $n + 1$ pairs $(u, v)$ of words with $uv = w$, ordered by the length of $u$: for each $i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ it contains the prefix of $w$ of length $i$ paired with the remaining suffix.

results.title: Recognizable languages are closed under concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be languages over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L_1$ and membership in $L_2$ are recognizable by multi-stack machines, then so is membership in the concatenation $L_1 L_2$, the set of words $uv$ with $u \in L_1$ and $v \in L_2$.

results.title: Extending a list of pieces by a letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a letter $a$ and a list $\pi = [u_1, \dots, u_k]$ of words, the extensions of $\pi$ by $a$ are listed as follows: first $[[a], u_1, \dots, u_k]$, which starts a new piece $[a]$, and then, only when $k \ge 1$, also $[a u_1, u_2, \dots, u_k]$, which puts the letter $a$ in front of the first piece.

results.title: Partitions of a word into nonempty factors
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $w$ over $\sigma$, this is the list of all ways to write $w$ as a concatenation $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ of nonempty words $u_1, \dots, u_k$, each recorded as the list $[u_1, \dots, u_k]$. The empty word has exactly one such partition, the empty list.

results.title: Recognizable languages are closed under Kleene star
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the Kleene star $L^*$, the set of all concatenations $u_1 \cdots u_k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_k \in L$.

results.title: Decidable languages are closed under Kleene star
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the Kleene star $L^*$, the set of all concatenations $u_1 \cdots u_k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_k \in L$.

results.title: Recognizable languages are closed under alphabet maps
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be alphabets with primitive recursive encodings, let $f : \sigma \to \tau$ be primitive recursive, and let $L$ be a language over $\sigma$. If membership in $L$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the image language $f(L) = \{f(a_1) \cdots f(a_n) : a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$, obtained by applying $f$ letter by letter to the words of $L$.

results.title: Sparse table
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A sparse table over a type $\alpha$ consists of an array of elements of $\alpha$, called its data, and an array of arrays of elements of $\alpha$, called its levels.

results.title: Option minimum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a type $\alpha$ with a minimum operation, the option minimum extends $\min$ to optional values (elements of $\alpha$ or none): on two elements $a, b$ of $\alpha$ it returns $\min(a, b)$, and none is a neutral element on either side.

results.title: Idempotence of the option minimum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and every optional value $a$ (an element of $\alpha$ or none), the option minimum of $a$ with itself is $a$.

results.title: Levels of a sparse table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $a$ over a type with a minimum operation $\min$, the levels of $a$ are defined recursively: level $0$ is $a$, and if level $k$ is $\ell = (\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{m-1})$, then level $k + 1$ is the list of the values $\min(\ell_i, \ell_{i+2^k})$ for $0 \le i < m - 2^k$ (empty when $m \le 2^k$).

results.title: Length of a level
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a list $a$ of length $n$ over a type with a minimum operation and a natural number $k$, level $k$ of $a$ has length $\max(n + 1 - 2^k, 0)$: one element for each start index $i$ with $i + 2^k \le n$.

results.title: Levels hold interval minima
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a linearly ordered type, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then level $k$ of $a$ has an element at index $i$, and it equals $\min(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_{i+2^k-1})$.

results.title: Next level of a sparse table row
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a type with a minimum operation, an array $(r_0, \dots, r_{n-1})$ and a natural number $k$, the next level is the array of length $n - 2^k$ (empty when $2^k \ge n$) whose entry $i$ is $\min(r_i, r_{i + 2^k})$.

results.title: One step of the sparse-table construction
results.caption: Definition

Given a pair $(r, L)$ of a current row $r$ (an array of length $|r|$) and an array $L$ of the rows recorded so far, and a natural number $k$, the build step returns the pair $(r', L')$, where $L'$ is $L$ with $r$ appended at the end, and $r'$ is the array whose entry $i$ is $\min(r_i, r_{i+2^k})$ for each $i$ with $i + 2^k < |r|$.

results.title: Built sparse tables are valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $a$ over a type with a minimum operation, the sparse table built from $a$ is valid: its stored rows are exactly the levels $0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ of $a$, in this order, where $n$ is the length of $a$ and $\lfloor \log_2 0 \rfloor$ is taken to be $0$.

results.title: Sparse-table entries
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sparse table $t$ and natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is element $i$ of the $k$-th stored row of $t$ (both counted from $0$) when $t$ has a $k$-th row and that row has an element at index $i$; otherwise the entry is undefined. Both lookups are random-access array lookups.

Then for every index $i$, the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is defined exactly when level $k$ of $d$ has an element at index $i$, and in that case the two are equal.

results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Entries of a valid sparse table are interval minima
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a linearly ordered type, with data $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{n-1})$, and let $k$ and $i$ be natural numbers with $i + 2^k \le n$. Then the entry of $t$ at row $k$ and index $i$ is defined and equals $\min(d_i, d_{i+1}, \dots, d_{i+2^k-1})$.

results.title: Sparse table range-minimum query
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sparse table $t$ over a type with a minimum operation and natural numbers $l, r$, the query over $[l, r)$ returns none when $r \le l$. Otherwise, with $k = \lfloor \log_2 (r - l) \rfloor$, it returns the option minimum (the minimum, with none as a neutral element on either side) of the entries of $t$ at level $k$ and indices $l$ and $r - 2^k$, in this order, where an entry not stored in $t$ counts as none.

results.title: Correctness of queries on valid sparse tables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a valid sparse table over a linearly ordered type whose data is the list $(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$, and let $l, r$ be natural numbers with $r \le n$. Then the range-minimum query over $[l, r)$ on $t$ returns the minimum of the slice $(a_l, \dots, a_{r-1})$ (none when $r \le l$, where the slice is empty).

results.title: Correctness of sparse table queries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list over a linearly ordered type and let $l, r$ be natural numbers with $r \le n$. Then the range-minimum query over $[l, r)$ on the sparse table built from $a$ returns the minimum of the slice $(a_l, \dots, a_{r-1})$ (none when $r \le l$, where the slice is empty).

results.title: Whole-range sparse table query
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $a$ of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, the range-minimum query over $[0, n)$ on the sparse table built from $a$ returns the minimum of $a$ (none when $a$ is empty).
